text: Access list items by their position, which we call the index — and Python starts counting at zero, not one.
[laugh] So index zero is apple, index one is banana, and index two is cherry.
That zero-based counting trips up a lot of beginners, so it's worth saying twice — the first item is always at index zero.
Negative indices count backward from the end, [gasp] so minus-one is the very last item.
And minus-two reaches the second-to-last, no need to know the list's length.
Indexing isn't just for lists — strings work exactly the same way, pulling out one character at a time.
[cough] But reach past the end of a list and Python raises an IndexError, which would normally crash your program.
So we wrap risky access in a try block and catch that error gracefully instead of crashing.
And if you know the value but not its position, the index method searches the list and hands you back exactly where it lives.
